title: California's Scott Wiener Has a Record of Opposing Gaza Ceasefire, Despite Recent Claim
author: Maria Blaze

During a congressional forum in January, the candidates vying to become the
Democratic nominee for California's 11th Congressional District were asked
whether they believed that Israel was committing a genocide in Gaza. San
Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and Saikat Chakrabarti both said "Yes." But
state Senator Scott Wiener himself declined to take a position on the
question. Within a few days the moment went viral online, sparking significant
backlash against his candidacy.

Later that week, he [announced on
X](https://x.com/Scott_Wiener/status/2010464312792404192?s=20) that he did, in
fact, believe that "Israel was committing a genocide in Gaza."

On Tuesday, San Franciscans will vote for their next congressional
representative. Wiener is leading in the
[polls](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-us-
house-11-polls-2026.html), but his about-face has led some voters to question
his position on Israel/Palestine and his likely political allegiances in
Washington, DC, should he become San Francisco's next congressional
representative.

In the years before October 7, 2023, Wiener criticized Prime Minister
Netanyahu, spoke out against the West Bank's settlement policy, and backed a
two-state solution. But according to his current campaign platform, he also
supports [arming Israel ](https://www.scottwiener.com/foreign-policy)with
defensive weapons and opposes the global Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS)
movement.

In a [CNN interview](https://www.cnn.com/2026/06/29/us/scott-wiener-gaza-
israel-california) over the summer, he falsely claimed that he has "supported
a ceasefire" in Gaza since November 2023. In fact, as late as December 2023,
he opposed a ceasefire. On December 5, 2023, the San Francisco Board of
Supervisors held a meeting to introduce the ceasefire resolution--which Wiener
opposed, alongside the Jewish Community Relations Council.

He did not merely voice his opposition to the measure. In the run-up to a
January 2024 vote on it, Wiener personally lobbied board members to oppose the
resolution, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Drop Site News.

And, despite rejecting AIPAC money this election cycle, he continues to accept
funding from liberal Zionist groups like J Street, which announced a [$60,000
ad campaign](https://jstreet.org/press-releases/j-street-action-fund-launches-
independent-expenditure-campaign-in-ca-11-primary-to-support-scott-wiener) to
support him in May 2026.

Wiener's office did not respond to a request for comment.

The ceasefire resolution that Wiener lobbied against ultimately passed 8-3,
thanks in part to the persistent advocacy of the Arab Resource and Organizing
Center (AROC). The group organized about 65,000 supporters, who sent emails to
the San Francisco Board of Supervisors to advocate for the resolution,
according to Lara Kiswani, AROC's executive director.

But Wiener's active opposition to the resolution undercuts the authenticity of
his politics, Kiswani told Drop Site News. "Plainly, it is a factual lie that
he supported the ceasefire since 2023," she said.

## Influencing the Classroom

A review of Wiener's record shows several noteworthy attempts to address
antisemitism, including advocacy and legislation that raise concerns around
censorship in education.

Wiener played a critical role in holding up funding for the state's ethnic
studies program, which was slated to become a graduation requirement for
public high school students. Because the program contained material about the
Nakba--the expulsion of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians beginning in
1947--and the BDS movement, the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, on which
Wiener served, pushed for guardrails that addressed concerns about "anti-
Jewish and anti-Israel bias."

[In a
letter](https://jewishcaucus.legislature.ca.gov/sites/jewishcaucus.legislature.ca.gov/files/190729%20Jewish%20Caucus%20Letter%20on%20Ethnic%20Studies%20Model%20Curriculum.pdf)
to a state committee that advises on educational material, the Jewish Caucus
said that anti-Jewish bias in the ethnic studies curriculum was "singling out
Israel--the world's only Jewish state--for special critique and condemnation."

Seth Morrison, a leader of the Bay Area chapter of Jewish Voice for Peace,
objected to the claim that the curriculum was anti-Jewish. "Israel is a
sovereign state. Judaism is a religion, not a nationality. Critiquing Israel
does not mean you are anti-Jewish," he said. "In fact, Israel's false claims
about representing all Jews actually perpetuates antisemitism."

In 2023, Wiener became co-chair of the Jewish Caucus, while also serving as
the Senate Budget and Fiscal Review Committee chair. His simultaneous
leadership in these roles has given him outsized power. Under his leadership,
the Jewish Caucus continued to insist on changes to the ethnic studies
curriculum, while as chair of the Budget Committee, Wiener influenced the
program's funding.

One state legislator, Rep. Al Muratsuchi, complained bitterly about the
opposition from Wiener and his allies. "We want to move the ethnic studies
high school graduation requirement forward," Muratsuchi, a former chair of the
Assembly Budget Committee on Education Finance, reportedly
[said](https://www.santacruzsentinel.com/2025/08/19/guest-commentary-sending-
maga-to-sacramento/). "But that is contingent on appropriation, and it just so
happens that the two co-chairs of the Jewish Caucus," Wiener and his colleague
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, "are both chairs of the budget committees of
both houses, the Senate and Assembly. And so we are dealing with complicated
politics on several levels."

An essential component of the campaign against the ethnic studies curriculum
was AB 715, which became law in October 2025. The legislation purports to
strengthen California's anti-discrimination policies in K-12 education, with a
focus on antisemitism. It was co-authored by Wiener and sponsored by the
California Legislative Jewish Caucus. Many teachers, including members of the
[California Faculty Association](https://www.calfac.org/cfa-members-denounce-
the-passing-of-assembly-bill-715-as-a-threat-to-free-speech-and-academic-
freedom-2/), have criticized the law as censoring instruction on topics like
Israel/Palestine.

Gabriel Kahn, an eighth-grade teacher in the Oakland Unified School District,
said that the law conflates antisemitism and criticism of Israel. "AB 715
creates an environment where teachers are scared to teach the truth and teach
current events as they are, particularly around Israel and Palestine," he told
Drop Site. "As a Jewish educator myself, Jewish educators and students are
already protected against antisemitism in our education code. What AB 715 does
is tag on criticism of Israel and Zionism to the definition of antisemitism."

Even students can be targeted under AB 715. In one case in April, a middle
school in Berkeley received a complaint after hosting a student-led assembly
that celebrated South and Southwest Asian and North African (SSWANA) cultures.
The complaint [alleged](https://jweekly.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/CDE-
decision-re-MLK-Jr.-Middle-School.pdf) that the SSWANA event "contributed to a
discriminatory and harassing environment for Jewish and Israeli students," the
California Department of Education [said](https://jweekly.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/CDE-decision-re-MLK-Jr.-Middle-School.pdf).

During the event, students displayed a PowerPoint presentation, seen by Drop
Site, that included a slide recognizing "some wars happening in our area,"
including "Palestinian genocide," "Sudan civil war," and "Israeli Invasion of
Southern Lebanon." The Department of Education, in its review of the event,
cited the school's finding that the assembly included "controversial content,"
including the mention of the genocide in Gaza and "Free Palestine" chants.

Ultimately, the department concluded that the complaint against the student
assembly had merit, and ordered the Berkeley Unified School District to take
"corrective actions." It said that the school must provide anti-discrimination
instruction to all students and administrators, "with a particular emphasis on
anti-Semitism."

Sahar Habib Ghazi, a parent of one of the students who organized the assembly,
told Drop Site that despite the complaint's centering of Israel, the issue was
secondary to the assembly. "Out of the many slides celebrating students'
culture, there was one slide focused on wars that were impacting some of our
students who are Palestinian, Lebanese, and Iranian. Because many kids were
being impacted by Israel's warfare, the slide became important."

On September 16, Ghazi's daughter, a student involved in the assembly, spoke
at a Berkeley Unified School Board meeting after the department's ruling.
"Thousands of us students came together to build something we're proud of,"
she said, according to a recording of the meeting. "Our culture gets treated
like something to be scared of, but because of that assembly my whole school
knew that I was Muslim and knew my family survived the British Partition of
India. CDE took that and turned it into a story about Israel and
antisemitism."

After publication, a spokesperson at the California Department of Education
told Drop Site that the department could not comment on the matter. "We cannot
comment on a California Department of Education (CDE) Uniform Complaint
Procedure appeal decision and must allow it to speak for itself," the
spokesperson, Scott Roark, said in a statement.

The organization K-12 Legal Defense is representing students who are
challenging the Department of Education decision against the school. Liz
Jackson, the group's legal director, said it was wrong for AB 715 to be
weaponized against a student-led assembly celebrating SSWANA culture. "I don't
want my Jewish kids to learn that celebrating SSWANA culture endangers them,"
she told Drop Site. "That's a deeply antisemitic lesson."

While Jackson said she was grateful to see Wiener's shift on Israel/Palestine,
she added that it did not go far enough. "Scott Wiener has steamrolled a
legislative agenda that promoted false and harmful myths around Palestinian
stories, equating it to antisemitism and therefore eliminating them from the
classroom," she said. "He may have changed his views, but he has not changed
the deep harm he enacted in our education system, which all students and
educators are left to cope with."

That harm is especially evident in the law's classroom censorship, Jackson
said. She noted that AB 715 permits any person to file a complaint over
educational practices in any school in the district. One need not be a
student, or even a resident of the city, to make a complaint. And the
legislation requires that every complaint is investigated by the school
district. Jackson said that this arrangement puts schools in a bind. "Because
the district knows that there are organizations with deep pockets ready to
litigate against them, they aren't gonna fight for students rights for
critical learning," she said. "They're just gonna take the posters down and
change the curriculum--that is the effect."

AB 715 was predated by another bill that Wiener co-authored, which restricts
protests and free speech in public universities. It became law in September
2024. Student advocates view the law, SB 1287, as an attempt to crack down on
campus demonstrations, especially those related to Israel/Palestine. It
imposes "time, place, and manner restrictions" on campus protests.

When Michael Lee-Chang was a student at California State University,
Sacramento, he was sanctioned for violating the school's "time, place, and
manner restrictions." He had allegedly placed stickers around campus that
criticized the university's chancellor, Mildred Garcia. Lee-Chang, who
recently graduated, said that the law, which the Jewish Caucus has described
as ensuring "Jewish safety," stifles campus protests.

When he was sanctioned by his school, Lee-Chang faced the possibility of
suspension. The process to resolve the sanction took several months. In the
end, the school issued a warning against him that will remain in his conduct
file for seven years.

_This story was updated to include a response from the California Department
of Education._
